query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: An enhanced predictive method that combines Debye temperature analysis with ab initio anharmonic phonon calculations and explicit local bonding/mass variance descriptors will more accurately identify high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibiting low lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys (e.g., FeCoCrMnNi and related compositions) with a homogeneous solid-solution state and measurable vibrational properties.
generation.intervention: Integrate the Callaway-Debye model with state-of-the-art ab initio anharmonic phonon/lattice dynamics calculations and incorporate local bonding descriptors (force constant fluctuations and mass variance) into the predictive framework.
generation.conditions: Evaluated over a wide temperature range spanning from 50 K up to high-temperature conditions (~1200 °C) where phonon scattering dominates.
generation.structural_mediator: Debye temperature together with local vibrational descriptors (bond-length variations and force-constant fluctuations) that mediate phonon propagation in disordered HEAs.
generation.mechanism: Alloy-induced anharmonicity, local bond strength variations, and mass disorder collectively lower the Debye temperature and phonon group velocity while enhancing scattering processes, thereby reducing lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA compositions with lower integrated Debye temperatures and significant local bonding disorder will exhibit reduced κL, with the model predicting thermal conductivity values with an expected error reduction of approximately 30% over traditional averaged-property models.
generation.baseline: Conventional predictive models based solely on averaged atomic masses and empirical Debye correlations.
generation.boundary: Applicable only to systems where phonon scattering dominates over electronic conduction; the approach may not be suitable for alloys with strong electron-mediated thermal transport.
generation.uncertainty: While incorporating local bonding and mass variance addresses concerns regarding oversimplification, the precise quantitative improvement (30% error reduction) remains uncertain; however, the integration of multiple descriptors is supported by recent experimental and computational studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a series of HEA compositions spanning a range of calculated integrated Debye temperatures and local bonding disorder metrics; measure their lattice thermal conductivities using established thermal analysis techniques and statistically compare the predicted values against experimental measurements.
measurements: Debye temperature (via specific heat and acoustic measurements)
Local bond fluctuation metrics (via high-resolution diffraction/TEM)
Lattice thermal conductivity (using laser flash or similar methods)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant inverse correlation between the integrated descriptors (Debye temperature plus local bonding metrics) and κL is observed, or if the model’s prediction error is not reduced by at least 30% relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We have calculated κL, κa, and κo using the Eqs. (S35), (S36) and (S37) respectively. Table 4 lists their values at 300 K. Figure 1f shows that m2, m5, and m8 have the lower κL among all other HE solid solutions. The Callaway-Debye theoretical model states that a higher ΘD indicates a higher thermal conductivity and vice versa. We plotted ΘD versus κ in Fig. S19a–d in SI to reveal the correlation between ΘD and κ. Figure S19 shows that ΘD is positively correlated with κ in agreement with Callaway-Debye model. The comparison between our calculated κ and κL with the experimental lattice thermal conductivity (κL)exp from Jiang’s work is listed in Table S10 showing similar trends. Melting temperature (Tmelt) is correlated to ΘD, κL, and thermal expansion. Materials with low Tmelt tend to have lower ΘD and higher thermal expansion. For high temperature applications such as thermoelectric applications, it is crucial to identify the thermal limits or melting temperature (Tmelt) of a material. More information about the formula used to calculate Tmelt can be found in (S38). The calculated Tmelt for m0 and nine solid solutions are presented in Table S10. m1, m5, and m8 have the lowest Tmelt

In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. If this is unexpected from Mu’s theory, which would predict increased force-constant fluctuations due to the larger variability of random environments of a given atomic pair, it explains recent experimental reports on comparable phonon lattice thermal conductivities in our HEA and FeNi
